comments.author: @shadfurman
comments.text:
AI doesn't make a copy, this is obvious on its face. The model isn't large enough to store all the information it's trained on. It wouldn't work if it was large enough, otherwise you wouldn't need to train it, you'd just use copies of the data and poof intelligence.

The intelligence comes from compressing the information into a model that's not big enough to store it, so that it has to develop heuristics to reconstruct a probable output.

It will memorize sections it's been trained on a lot, if it occurs often in its data, and while this is useful sometimes you do want exact quotes sometimes, it's called ovetfitting and generally considered a negative in model development, because memorization is not understanding, and for most cases indicates the model is too large for the amount of data.

comments.author: @nuxof
comments.text: Lawyers, please understand that any downloading/reading of online data is copying. If you tokenize the data, it is transforming it into a different format, but it can still be converted back to represent the same content. This is similar to encoding it (base64, mime, binary etc.), encrypting (TLS/SSL for safe transfer etc.) it and even translating it to a different language. If the courts accepted that tokenization is not copying, then they need to read up on their technology or hire technical consultants. In all fairness, I believe the analogy of AIs learning from human works in the same way humans do (by going to the library, listening to radio/tv/youtube etc.) is a very good and precise analogy. Otherwise, AI would be the best compression algorithm ever invented (being able to compress the entirety of the Internet down to a few billion parameters).

comments.author: @kingsridge
comments.text:
What's crazy is half of this problem exists because of anthropomorphized computational terms. AI's don't "study or train" to do anything. And if these cases were seen as INPUT/OUTPUT instead of talking about ChapGPT  like it got good at Art during a gap year in Europe, this wouldn't even be a conversation. Machines don't use the visual light spectrum to interpret the world. Words, pictures, and sounds are 0s and 1s.  Regardless of whether a machine COPIES and stores a data set at once--or processes that data in part, or out of sequence, over multiple passes--it retains the information it combed in a perpetually perfect state that humans cannot. 

I can be cynical. But even I've had a hard time perceiving the audacity it takes to 100% steal peoples' talent on a global scale,  and gaslight them about it, while pursuing legal goals that makes it impossible for the people to ever fully own/profit exclusively from their work. A better question than "What is 'copying'???" --is why would anyone be OK with the continual scraping of human work that said humans wish not to be scraped for AI input.
